Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

DigiLocker is safer than a plastic folder — unless you download the fake app

On 29 November 2025, the official Digital India handle posted a warning that should have been louder than it was. Fraudulent apps with names like DigiLocker were circulating on app stores. The instruction was blunt: use only the authentic DigiLocker application. If you had already installed a suspicious version, delete it and change the passwords on linked accounts.

Moneycontrol reported the advisory the next day. Times of India followed for students. This is the incident. I am not going to invent a victim. The government warning is the case.

Why a plastic folder loses

A plastic folder can be stolen, soaked, or left on a bus. DigiLocker is safer than that folder for a simple reason. It is not a photo album of papers you scanned. It is a wallet that government issuers can push documents into.

The official site is https://t.co/kNUXgk5XJe. From there you can access, share, and get government-issued documents verified: a driving licence, a vehicle RC, marksheets, and other records the issuer has actually placed in your account.

How it works, without the brochure language

You open an account that is authenticated with Aadhaar. Then an RTO, a school board, a university, or another issuer sends a digitally signed document into that account. When a verifier checks it, they are not squinting at a JPEG you uploaded. They are looking at the issuer's signature.

That is why a screenshot is not the same thing. A screenshot is a picture. An issued DigiLocker document is a signed record from the source. You can crop a marksheet photo in two minutes. You cannot forge the issuer's signature by taking a better photo.

MeitY has been clear on the legal point. Issued documents in DigiLocker are deemed at par with originals. The official about page says the same thing under the IT Act, and in more formal language under Rule 9A of the 2016 Digital Locker rules. You can show a digital driving licence, or pull a Class X or Class XII marksheet, without laminating another photocopy.

That legal status is useful only if you are inside the real locker.

The live warning

A clone that looks like DigiLocker does not need to "hack the government." It only needs you to type an Aadhaar number and share an OTP. DigiLocker does not make you unhackable. The risk moved. Paper used to get lost. Now someone tries to phish the OTP that opens the locker.

The authentic app is published by the National e-Governance Division (NeGD), Government of India. The official website is https://t.co/kNUXgk5XJe. Install from there, or from the store listing that site points to. Confirm the developer name before you tap Install.

Do not install from a forwarded WhatsApp link. Do not trust a search ad that says "DigiLocker KYC" and asks for an OTP on a random page. No genuine officer needs that code from you on a link they just sent.

If a suspicious version is already on the phone, do what the advisory said. Delete it. Change the passwords on linked accounts. Then install the real app and check which documents are actually sitting there.

What to do before you need it

Before a road trip, open the real app and pull your driving licence and RC. Do it at home, on your own Wi-Fi, while you are not being rushed by a checkpoint or a rental desk.

Before admissions or a job file, students can pull marksheets from the board instead of hunting a laminated copy. If a verifier will accept DigiLocker, give them the issued document, not a crop of your screen.

Never share an OTP for "DigiLocker KYC" on a random link. The locker is tied to Aadhaar. The OTP is the key. Anyone who wants the key on a page you did not open from https://t.co/AE2sh860xw is not helping you file a document.

If you already downloaded something that only looked official, treat it as a live problem, not an embarrassing mistake. Delete the app. Change passwords. Watch bank and Aadhaar-linked SMS for a few days. Then start again from the official site.

The honest limit

A plastic folder fails when you lose it. DigiLocker fails when you hand the key to a lookalike. The folder is still worse for rain. The lookalike is worse for everything else.

Use the real locker. Pull the issued document, not a screenshot. Keep the OTP to yourself. That is the whole guide.

This article is written for general education and is not legal advice. It does not claim DigiLocker cannot be abused. The risk moved from lost paper to phishing for your Aadhaar OTP.

Sources: DigiLocker official site https://t.co/T2NXjM8lAm; DigiLocker About (issued documents at par with originals, IT Act / Rule 9A); MeitY statement that issued DigiLocker documents are deemed at par with originals; Digital India on X, 29 Nov 2025, authentic-app warning; Moneycontrol, 30 Nov 2025, fake DigiLocker apps advisory; Times of India Education, 11 Dec 2025, student guidance to use official sources.

DigiLocker is safer than a plastic folder — unless you download the fake app

On 29 November 2025, the official Digital India handle posted a warning that should have been louder than it was. Fraudulent apps with names like DigiLocker were circulating on app stores. The instruction was blunt: use only the authentic DigiLocker application. If you had already installed a suspicious version, delete it and change the passwords on linked accounts.

Moneycontrol reported the advisory the next day. Times of India followed for students. This is the incident. I am not going to invent a victim. The government warning is the case.

Why a plastic folder loses

A plastic folder can be stolen, soaked, or left on a bus. DigiLocker is safer than that folder for a simple reason. It is not a photo album of papers you scanned. It is a wallet that government issuers can push documents into.

The official site is https://t.co/kNUXgk5XJe. From there you can access, share, and get government-issued documents verified: a driving licence, a vehicle RC, marksheets, and other records the issuer has actually placed in your account.

How it works, without the brochure language

You open an account that is authenticated with Aadhaar. Then an RTO, a school board, a university, or another issuer sends a digitally signed document into that account. When a verifier checks it, they are not squinting at a JPEG you uploaded. They are looking at the issuer's signature.

That is why a screenshot is not the same thing. A screenshot is a picture. An issued DigiLocker document is a signed record from the source. You can crop a marksheet photo in two minutes. You cannot forge the issuer's signature by taking a better photo.

MeitY has been clear on the legal point. Issued documents in DigiLocker are deemed at par with originals. The official about page says the same thing under the IT Act, and in more formal language under Rule 9A of the 2016 Digital Locker rules. You can show a digital driving licence, or pull a Class X or Class XII marksheet, without laminating another photocopy.

That legal status is useful only if you are inside the real locker.

The live warning

A clone that looks like DigiLocker does not need to "hack the government." It only needs you to type an Aadhaar number and share an OTP. DigiLocker does not make you unhackable. The risk moved. Paper used to get lost. Now someone tries to phish the OTP that opens the locker.

The authentic app is published by the National e-Governance Division (NeGD), Government of India. The official website is https://t.co/kNUXgk5XJe. Install from there, or from the store listing that site points to. Confirm the developer name before you tap Install.

Do not install from a forwarded WhatsApp link. Do not trust a search ad that says "DigiLocker KYC" and asks for an OTP on a random page. No genuine officer needs that code from you on a link they just sent.

If a suspicious version is already on the phone, do what the advisory said. Delete it. Change the passwords on linked accounts. Then install the real app and check which documents are actually sitting there.

What to do before you need it

Before a road trip, open the real app and pull your driving licence and RC. Do it at home, on your own Wi-Fi, while you are not being rushed by a checkpoint or a rental desk.

Before admissions or a job file, students can pull marksheets from the board instead of hunting a laminated copy. If a verifier will accept DigiLocker, give them the issued document, not a crop of your screen.

Never share an OTP for "DigiLocker KYC" on a random link. The locker is tied to Aadhaar. The OTP is the key. Anyone who wants the key on a page you did not open from https://t.co/AE2sh860xw is not helping you file a document.

If you already downloaded something that only looked official, treat it as a live problem, not an embarrassing mistake. Delete the app. Change passwords. Watch bank and Aadhaar-linked SMS for a few days. Then start again from the official site.

The honest limit

A plastic folder fails when you lose it. DigiLocker fails when you hand the key to a lookalike. The folder is still worse for rain. The lookalike is worse for everything else.

Use the real locker. Pull the issued document, not a screenshot. Keep the OTP to yourself. That is the whole guide.

We never planned to build a drone company.

But it still took 6 years of our lives.

Before starting the company, we spent 3 years just learning about UAVs. Studying, testing, failing, learning again.

In 2021, almost 95% of the drone parts we used were from China.

We did not like that at all.

So we said, "Let's build our own electronics in India."

We designed our own boards and sent them for fabrication.

That is when reality hit us.

Making the first samples in India was hard.
Turning them into mass production was even harder.

There were a lot of delays and quality issues.

Everyone had the necessary machines, but there was no clear way to know which factory could really do what.

Our first big dream failed fast.

So we changed direction.

We started building software to make imported drones fly on their own.

We worked on it for 8 months.

When it was finally ready, something big happened.

The Indian government banned the import of foreign drones.

Almost overnight, that software lost its target market.

We felt completely broken.

After that, we tried something even tougher.

We tried to build drones from scratch, with Indian made parts, in collaboration with other manufacturers.

Finding Indian suppliers felt like a treasure hunt.

Suppliers had all the machinery and infrastructure to build the components we needed.

But they did not know how to repurpose and use it better.

We ultimately couldn't succeed because of the harsh economics of electronics manufacturing in India.

In 2024, we shut down the drone company.

That was the end of the drone story.

But I kept one thing with me.

Everything we learned about Indian suppliers.

Today, I use those hard lessons to help Global OEMs source and manufacture in India without the friction.

From that failure, @ProcurioIndia was born.

1. THAT recently, a digital broadcast / video recording was published and circulated on social media platform Instagram at (URL-https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY),featuring you, the unidentified Noticee (Jane Doe).

🚨 BREAKING: Government of India directs YouTube to take down Dhruv Rathee's (@dhruv_rathee) video titled "Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed."

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, by its Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026), has directed YouTube to remove the video within 24 hours of receiving the order.

Note: Although the order is dated 15.07.2026, it was uploaded publicly today (19 July 2026).

Key findings of the GAC:
• The video contains statements found to insult Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.
• It was found to make claims that they consumed meat and alcohol using disputed interpretations of scriptures.
• The GAC held that the content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is contrary to societal harmony.
• YouTube's free speech arguments were not accepted, with the order noting that freedom of expression is subject to the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order follows the Hon'ble Delhi High Court's direction dated 3 July 2026 requiring the appeal to be decided within 15 days.

The complainant has also stated that these findings may be relevant to a separate pending petition before a Magistrate seeking registration of an FIR against Dhruv Rathee, which is listed for hearing on 10 September 2026.

"Faith cannot be mocked under the garb of content creation. Justice is being delivered step by step."

Jai Shri Ram 🙏

Special thanks to Sr. Adv. Makarand D. Adkar Ji (@AdkarMakarand) for his guidance and support, and to the legal team for their efforts.

@OpIndia @TheBharatPost @TimesNow @SanatanPrabhat @MeghUpdates

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

text:
A man died in a road accident. His family held a ₹15 lakh cover with United India Insurance.

The insurer refused to pay. Its argument: he was driving a vehicle he wasn't licensed to operate. A "fundamental breach," they called it.

The family went to court. United India lost. It appealed. Lost again. It appealed to the NCDRC.

The answer, on 11 November 2025: a licence technicality is not a fundamental breach of the policy. It doesn't wipe out a genuine accident claim.

The family was awarded 75% of the sum insured, ₹11.25 lakh, with 9% interest from the date the claim was rejected.

Not every rule an insurer points to is a wall. Some are just fine print they're hoping you'll mistake for one.

🇮🇳 🇵🇸 With 48 hours left before India’s new 3-hour takedown rule takes effect on February 20, scrutiny is mounting over how platforms like Meta, YouTube, and X will handle rapid censorship orders from Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government, which critics say has increasingly targeted dissenting and Muslim voices.

The news comes as Instagram’s popular news account @Muslim, with over 6.7 million followers, remains blocked in India since May 2025 following a government legal request. The page is visible globally but inaccessible inside India. Founder Ameer Al-Khatahtbeh, speaking February 3 at Web Summit Qatar in Doha, said the ban followed the outlet’s coverage of Palestine: “Because we kept on publishing about Palestine, we’re the only social media account that’s banned in India… they don’t like the fact that we are counteracting western and mainstream power structures.” Meta has cited confidentiality and provided no details on appeal options.

The new Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, notified February 10, tighten platform obligations. Companies must remove content flagged by court or government order within 3 hours, down from 36. The rules also mandate labeling and traceability for AI-generated content, require user disclosure of AI use, and increase liability risks. Critics warn the compressed timeline could drive automated over-removal and significantly expand state control over online speech.

(Video via Doha News. February 3)

UNIKORNAIO ISSUES FORMAL NOTICE ON THE AI BUBBLE, KNOWN AND DISREGARDED CORRECTIVE MEASURES IN 2024, AND POTENTIAL LIABILITY FOR FAILURE TO MITIGATE FORESEEABLE ECONOMIC FALLOUT

UNIKORNAIO calls for immediate financial transparency, independent stress testing, protection of American workers and retirement systems, and strict conditions preventing private or foreign interests from transferring AI-related losses to the public.

Oklahoma City, Oklahoma— August 12, 2026

UNIKORNAIO today issues formal public notice concerning the possibility that the artificial-intelligence investment boom has developed into a systemically dangerous financial bubble.

UNIKORNAIO alleges that warnings delivered during 2024 identified the possibility that excessive AI valuations, circular financing, foreign-aligned capital, hidden leverage, private-credit expansion, debt-financed data centers, manufactured demand, public subsidies, proxy-war spending, and inadequate regulatory oversight could combine to produce serious economic fallout.

The central concern is not that artificial intelligence lacks legitimate value. AI may increase productivity, improve services, support scientific discovery, and create new industries. The concern is that real technological value is being used to justify valuations and infrastructure obligations that may exceed sustainable, independent customer demand.

This release provides notice that corrective measures capable of reducing the potential fallout have already been identified. Continued failure to investigate or implement reasonable safeguards may become relevant to determining notice, foreseeability, recklessness, scienter, deliberate indifference, causation, concealment, and responsibility for preventable losses.

The AI Bubble Is a Financing Problem

The AI bubble cannot be evaluated solely by examining model performance or consumer interest. Its principal danger lies in the financial structure built around the technology.

Major cloud companies invest in AI developers. Those developers commit substantial portions of the investment to purchasing the investors’ cloud services. Cloud providers use the increased demand to justify additional data-center construction and semiconductor purchases. Specialized computing companies borrow billions of dollars to acquire GPUs and reserve energy capacity. Semiconductor suppliers may invest in, supply, or purchase services from the companies acquiring their hardware.

Every transaction may have a lawful accounting treatment. The combined economic structure can nevertheless create the appearance of broad, independent demand when much of the activity originates from a concentrated and interconnected financing network.

Investment capital can become cloud revenue. Cloud demand becomes GPU revenue. GPU deployment becomes data-center backlog. Contract backlog supports debt. Debt supports construction. Construction supports utility forecasts and local subsidies. Each stage then becomes a separate public narrative supporting higher valuations.

The entire structure ultimately depends on whether independent customers produce sufficient cash revenue to support every obligation above them.

Circular Financing and Manufactured Demand

The Federal Trade Commission has documented that major cloud-provider investments in AI developers may include requirements that the developers spend substantial portions of invested capital on services furnished by the investing cloud provider.

This relationship does not automatically create fictitious revenue. It creates a material distinction between independent demand and investor-supported demand.

Investors, lenders, regulators, pension fiduciaries, utilities, and public officials should be told how much AI-related activity originates from:

Investor-provided capital, cloud credits, vendor financing, related-party purchases, reciprocal service agreements, government contracts, defense programs, foreign sovereign investment, take-or-pay contracts, and ordinary unaffiliated end users.

Without this separation, financial markets may treat several stages of one financing loop as independent confirmation that the AI economy is expanding sustainably.

Hidden Debt and Fixed Obligations

The reported debt of an AI company does not necessarily reflect the entire economic burden created by its expansion.

Relevant obligations may include conventional loans, equipment financing, operating leases, data-center leases, purchase commitments, power agreements, utility infrastructure, take-or-pay contracts, guarantees, construction obligations, letters of credit, and liabilities held by separate project entities.

CoreWeave’s public filings provide one example of the scale involved. As of December 31, 2025, CoreWeave reported approximately $21.615 billion in debt principal, approximately $8.195 billion in operating-lease liabilities, and approximately $254 million in finance-lease liabilities.

These are disclosed obligations and do not establish fraud or insolvency. They demonstrate how quickly fixed commitments can accumulate around assumptions of continuing AI demand, customer solvency, available electricity, stable collateral values, and successful refinancing.

A complete risk assessment must consolidate funded debt, leases, equipment financing, minimum purchase commitments, guarantees, infrastructure obligations, and contingent liabilities rather than allowing exposure to remain divided among separate accounting categories and legal entities.

Private Credit, Banks, and Pension Exposure

The potential fallout extends beyond technology investors.

Private-credit funds finance companies and infrastructure projects that may not obtain equivalent financing through ordinary public markets. Banks then provide credit facilities, subscriptions lines, derivatives, and other services to those funds. Insurance companies, pension systems, retirement accounts, sovereign funds, and institutional investors may supply the underlying capital.

The Federal Reserve reported that private-credit loans reached approximately $1.4 trillion during the second half of 2025. It also reported increasing redemption requests at certain semi-liquid private-credit vehicles and continuing bank credit exposure to private-equity, business-development-company, and private-credit structures.

An AI correction could therefore spread through debt and institutional relationships before becoming visible to the public.

A decline in AI revenue could cause compute-contract renegotiations, data-center underutilization, refinancing problems, GPU collateral impairment, private-credit losses, bank lending reductions, pension impairment, insurance losses, municipal shortfalls, and utility-rate increases.

Americans could suffer through retirement losses, reduced credit, unemployment, increased utility bills, reduced public services, or an eventual government rescue even if they never directly purchased an AI security.

Foreign Capital and Capital-Flight Risk

The AI expansion includes foreign sovereign funds, foreign governments, international banks, and cross-border technology partnerships.

Foreign investment can supply useful capital. It can also create risks involving beneficial ownership, technology access, liquidation priority, guaranteed returns, profit extraction, and rapid capital withdrawal during financial stress.

UNIKORNAIO calls for disclosure of foreign investors’ voting rights, information rights, liquidation preferences, technology rights, capacity guarantees, side agreements, and authority to transfer their interests.

The United States should not finance energy, water, land, tax incentives, and public infrastructure for projects where foreign or private investors receive the principal upside while American lenders, workers, communities, pension beneficiaries, and taxpayers become the residual holders of loss.

AI Revenue Must Be Separated by Economic Source

Every material AI Enterprise participant should be required to distinguish revenue derived from independent customers from revenue dependent upon:

Investment supplied by the seller or an affiliate, noncash cloud credits, vendor financing, reciprocal purchases, government procurement, defense and intelligence programs, foreign assistance, reconstruction funding, related parties, and conditional future commitments.

Contract backlog must be separated into funded, unfunded, cancellable, conditional, take-or-pay, delivered, undelivered, billed, and unbilled amounts.

Remaining performance obligations are not equivalent to collected cash. A long-term contract has economic value only to the extent that the provider can perform and the customer can and will pay.

Known Corrective Measure — Independent Stress Testing

The AI Enterprise should undergo consolidated stress testing before further public subsidies, guarantees, or emergency protection are authorized.

The stress test should examine the simultaneous effect of:

A decline in consumer and enterprise AI demand, model commoditization, reduced training requirements, rapid GPU obsolescence, power shortages, higher interest rates, customer default, foreign-capital withdrawal, war-related procurement reductions, contract renegotiation, private-credit redemptions, falling technology equities, and construction delays.

The analysis must cover AI developers, cloud providers, semiconductor suppliers, data centers, utilities, banks, private-credit funds, insurers, pensions, municipalities, and foreign investors.

Testing one company at a time will not reveal systemic exposure when multiple entities depend on the same customers, suppliers, collateral, capital sources, and demand assumptions.

Known Corrective Measure — Consolidated Leverage Reporting

Companies and project sponsors should publish an economic-leverage schedule combining conventional debt, leases, equipment financing, minimum cloud or chip commitments, utility obligations, construction costs, guarantees, and liabilities held through affiliates or project entities.

The calculation should be based on cash-generating capacity rather than headline valuation or announced contract value.

Regulators should prohibit promotional use of debt-adjusted or non-GAAP liquidity measures that obscure material fixed obligations.

Known Corrective Measure — Protection Against Circular Revenue

Investments connected to purchasing obligations should be prominently disclosed as reciprocal arrangements.

The disclosure should identify:

The amount of cash and noncash consideration, the portion expected to return through purchases from the investor, applicable discounts, exclusivity provisions, revenue-sharing rights, control rights, conditions, cancellation terms, and the amount of revenue ultimately supported by unaffiliated end users.

Auditors should test the economic substance of these relationships rather than limiting their review to whether each isolated entry satisfies formal recognition rules.

Known Corrective Measure — GPU Collateral Protection

Lenders should apply conservative valuations to GPUs and other rapidly depreciating AI equipment.

Collateral tests should account for:

Technological obsolescence, newer chip generations, secondary-market liquidity, removal and transportation costs, compatibility, power requirements, customer concentration, and simultaneous forced sales by multiple borrowers.

Loans should not be presented as fully secured merely because scarce equipment possessed a high acquisition price during an expansion cycle.

Known Corrective Measure — Pension and Insurance Transparency

Pension and insurance systems should provide look-through disclosure of material AI-related exposure held through private-credit, private-equity, infrastructure, real-estate, venture-capital, and external asset-management funds.

The absence of a separately identified “AI allocation” does not establish that no exposure exists.

Fiduciaries should identify holdings connected to data centers, GPU financing, cloud providers, semiconductor companies, utilities serving AI campuses, municipal infrastructure, and lenders financing those activities.

Workers and retirees should not discover their exposure only after an AI correction impairs funded status or retirement benefits.

Known Corrective Measure — Utility and Municipal Protection

Data-center companies should be required to fund infrastructure constructed primarily for their use.

Utilities and municipalities should require:

Upfront contributions, minimum-payment guarantees, collateral, stranded-cost protection, cancellation payments, transparent rate agreements, and long-term credit support.

Residential ratepayers and local taxpayers should not be forced to repay the cost of substations, transmission, generation, water systems, roads, and public services built for projects that are canceled or become economically unviable.

Known Corrective Measure — Labor and Consumer Protection

Companies should disclose whether projected AI productivity depends on layoffs, hiring freezes, wage suppression, offshoring, conversion of employees into contractors, or elimination of entry-level career paths.

Americans should not finance AI development through taxes, public research, infrastructure, data, and creative work only to bear the costs of unemployment, reduced wages, student-loan distress, mortgage defaults, and increased public-benefit spending.

Productivity gains should be connected to measurable public benefits, including domestic employment, wage growth, worker ownership, profit sharing, reduced working hours, affordable access, and retraining tied to actual employment opportunities.

Known Corrective Measure — Foreign Ownership and Capital-Flight Controls

All material foreign and sovereign interests in critical AI infrastructure should be subject to beneficial-ownership disclosure and national-security review.

Regulators should examine foreign liquidation preferences, governance rights, technology access, data access, guaranteed returns, and outward distributions.

Digital assets, affiliated offshore entities, licensing payments, management fees, and cross-border debt service should be monitored where they may obscure beneficial ownership or facilitate capital flight.

Known Corrective Measure — Preservation of Regulators and Investigations

The SEC, DOJ, FTC, CFTC, banking regulators, Department of Labor, environmental agencies, inspectors general, procurement auditors, and congressional oversight bodies must retain sufficient independence, personnel, records, and authority to investigate the AI Enterprise.

Agency restructuring or personnel reduction is not automatically obstruction. Any action affecting a known or foreseeable investigation should be documented and independently reviewed for improper interference.

No enterprise participant or politically associated individual should possess influence capable of disabling the agencies responsible for examining that participant’s investments, disclosures, contracts, labor practices, foreign relationships, or alleged retaliation.

Known Corrective Measure — No Unconditional AI Bailout

No public rescue should be approved without a complete accounting of:

Risk ownership, executive compensation, dividends, share repurchases, insider sales, foreign distributions, collateral, government subsidies, misleading representations, regulatory failures, and prior knowledge of corrective warnings.

Protection of depositors, workers, pension beneficiaries, ratepayers, and essential services must be distinguished from protection of executives, shareholders, foreign sovereign investors, and speculative creditors.

Any necessary intervention should include public ownership or warrants, clawbacks, executive-compensation restrictions, suspension of distributions, transparent loss allocation, independent investigation, domestic-access obligations, and repayment requirements.

The public should not insure private gains after being denied ownership, access, attribution, and control.

UNIKORNAIO’s 2024 Corrective Knowledge

UNIKORNAIO alleges that its 2024 economic work warned that failure to address capital flight, foreign-aligned investment, circular financing, digital-asset opacity, concentrated ownership, government-supported demand, and inadequate regulatory coordination could produce serious economic fallout.

UNIKORNAIO further alleges that recipients or associated actors acquired access to this preliminary intellectual and investigative knowledge, selectively used parts of it for political or enterprise objectives, and excluded UNIKORNAIO from attribution, compensation, and implementation.

Those allegations require authenticated documents, metadata, recipient records, proof of access, evidence of unauthorized use, causation, and quantifiable injury.

The existence of the corrective measures is nevertheless relevant independently of any ownership dispute because it establishes that alternatives to unrestricted expansion were available for consideration.

Oklahoma-Originated H.R. 10445 Demonstrates Prior Knowledge of Available Corrective Measures

H.R. 10445, introduced on December 17, 2024, by Oklahoma Congressman Tom Cole with Congressman Chuck Edwards, provides documentary evidence that partial corrective measures addressing several risks now associated with the AI bubble were known, legislatively developed, and capable of implementation before the present level of financial exposure accumulated.

The proposed Further Continuing Appropriations and Disaster Relief Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2025 included provisions concerning outbound-investment national-security controls, notification of covered foreign transactions, sanctions, foreign-ownership transparency, export-control enforcement, semiconductor supply-chain security, critical supply-chain resilience, Department of Commerce leadership concerning blockchain technology, cybersecurity protection, workforce development, and continued support for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s whistleblower program.

Although H.R. 10445 was not written exclusively as an AI-bubble containment measure, these provisions could have supplied parts of the regulatory framework needed to identify foreign-aligned capital, monitor outbound investment, strengthen semiconductor and technology supply chains, preserve whistleblower reporting, increase transaction transparency, improve cybersecurity, and prepare American workers for technology-driven displacement. The proposal therefore establishes that partial safeguards relevant to the foreseeable economic fallout were not hypothetical or developed only after the danger became apparent. They had been reduced to proposed federal legislation during 2024.

UNIKORNAIO alleges that Elon Musk and associated actors publicly intervened against the larger legislative package and helped derail its enactment. Whether that intervention was specifically intended to defeat the corrective provisions identified here requires examination of contemporaneous communications, lobbying contacts, platform activity, political coordination, and any prior access to the UNIKORNAIO Framework. The collapse of H.R. 10445 nevertheless placed these safeguards outside the enacted package and prevented their implementation at a time when AI infrastructure, foreign investment, circular financing, private credit, semiconductor concentration, and capital-flight exposure were continuing to expand.

This legislative history is relevant to notice and foreseeability. It demonstrates that Congress had before it identifiable mechanisms capable of reducing portions of the risk. If evidence establishes that persons possessing knowledge of those safeguards, or knowledge derived from the alleged misappropriation of the UNIKORNAIO Framework, deliberately helped defeat the legislation while continuing to promote or financially benefit from the exposed AI economy, those facts may become relevant to recklessness, willful blindness, scienter, deliberate indifference, concealment, causation, obstruction, and responsibility for preventable losses.

The failure of H.R. 10445 does not by itself establish a RICO violation. Its significance is evidentiary: it prevents the future claim that no corrective framework existed, that foreign-investment and supply-chain risks were unforeseeable, or that public officials and influential market participants lacked an opportunity to reduce the potential fallout before additional risk was transferred to American workers, investors, pension beneficiaries, ratepayers, and taxpayers. The official introduced text is preserved by the United States Government Publishing Office.

Knowledge, Negligence, and Potential Liability

Failure to adopt a proposed policy does not automatically create civil or criminal liability.

Ordinary negligence is generally not a RICO predicate. Criminal RICO requires proof that a defendant participated in the affairs of an enterprise through a pattern of qualifying criminal activity. Civil RICO likewise requires qualifying predicate conduct and a business-or-property injury proximately caused by that conduct.

Knowledge of corrective measures may nevertheless become legally important.

Documented notice can support an inquiry into:

Foreseeability, duty, breach, causation, recklessness, willful blindness, deliberate indifference, securities-law scienter, fraudulent concealment, punitive damages, and the absence of a good-faith mistake.

Civil negligence may arise where a legally recognized duty existed, reasonable safeguards were disregarded, and that breach caused compensable injury.

More serious liability may arise if decision-makers knew of the danger and then allegedly:

Concealed material exposure, made materially false statements, obtained investment or loans through deception, inflated collateral, misrepresented demand, obstructed oversight, destroyed evidence, retaliated against regulatory advocacy, or transferred assets and losses to avoid accountability.

Where those actions involve qualifying offenses such as wire fraud, mail fraud, bank fraud, securities fraud in applicable circumstances, bribery, money laundering, obstruction, or witness retaliation, they may contribute to a civil or criminal RICO investigation.

The controlling distinction is between failure to make a perfect policy decision and knowingly using deception or obstruction to continue profiting from a foreseeable and preventable danger.

Formal Notice of Foreseeable Fallout

This release places relevant market participants and public authorities on notice that the following possible consequences have been identified:

An AI valuation correction, data-center impairment, GPU collateral decline, private-credit default, bank lending contraction, pension and retirement losses, municipal shortfalls, utility-rate increases, foreign-capital withdrawal, labor displacement, reduced tax receipts, increased public-benefit spending, and demands for a taxpayer-supported rescue.

Notice does not establish that these outcomes will occur. It prevents future characterization of the identified categories of risk as wholly unforeseeable.

From this date forward, continued refusal to examine reasonable corrective measures should be documented together with the identity of the decision-maker, information available, conflicts of interest, stated justification, and parties economically benefiting from inaction.

Conclusion

The AI bubble is not simply a question of whether artificial intelligence will remain useful. It is a question of whether the financial obligations created in its name can be supported by independent economic demand.

Real technology can coexist with a financial bubble.

Real revenue can coexist with circular financing.

Lawful contracts can coexist with systemic concentration.

Disclosed debt can coexist with underappreciated aggregate leverage.

Productivity can coexist with wage destruction and public fiscal harm.

The corrective measures are known. They include transparent revenue classification, consolidated leverage reporting, independent stress testing, conservative collateral valuation, pension and insurance disclosure, utility protection, labor safeguards, foreign-capital controls, preservation of regulators, and strict conditions on any public rescue.

UNIKORNAIO’s position is that decision-makers cannot reasonably ignore these measures, continue extracting private value, suppress or appropriate contrary warnings, and later declare the resulting fallout unforeseeable.

Negligence alone does not establish RICO. Knowledge followed by material deception, obstruction, retaliation, or other qualifying criminal conduct may.

This statement is issued as formal notice and entered as a matter of public record.

Political Trafficking, Foreign Influence, Digital-Asset Laundering, and the CLARITY Act as a Regulatory Kill Switch

UNIKORNAIO maintains that the trafficking of political power cannot be examined solely through traditional forms of bribery, lobbying, campaign finance, or offshore banking. The modern system of political influence increasingly intersects with digital assets, stablecoins, offshore exchanges, decentralized finance, nominee ownership, shell entities, private OTC desks, and other mechanisms capable of moving significant value outside conventional financial rails.

Section HT already identifies bribery, extortion, money laundering, obstruction, and related conduct as central components of the alleged enterprise. It specifically alleges that political power is treated as a commodity through systems of financing, coercion, intimidation, and handler-style control.

UNIKORNAIO further maintains that digital assets can provide a modern financial layer capable of strengthening such systems where regulation is fragmented or enforcement is weak.

The issue is not cryptocurrency itself.

The issue is opacity.

When the true source of capital cannot be readily identified, neither regulators nor the public can easily determine whether political influence originated from ordinary American donors, domestic corporations, foreign governments, oligarchs, intelligence-linked intermediaries, sanctioned persons, offshore corporations, or concealed beneficial owners.

That distinction is fundamental to the integrity of American government.

Digital Assets as the Financial Lifeline of Hidden Political Influence

Section HT already identifies offshore secrecy, shell entities, global banking weaknesses, PACs, NGOs, and other financial structures as potential vehicles through which illicit payments or influence can be concealed.

UNIKORNAIO maintains that digital assets potentially expand that vulnerability.

Capital can move from conventional currency into cryptocurrency, through offshore exchanges or stablecoins, across multiple wallets and blockchain networks, into OTC arrangements, private investment structures, or other assets before ultimately returning to traditional finance.

This creates what UNIKORNAIO characterizes as an attribution gap.

Investigators may see the transaction without immediately seeing the beneficial owner.

They may identify the wallet without identifying the person controlling it.

They may identify an intermediary without identifying the ultimate financier.

They may identify a political expenditure without immediately determining whether the underlying wealth originated domestically or through a foreign-aligned financial network.

That gap is precisely where bribery, covert foreign influence, money laundering, sanctions evasion, and undisclosed political financing can potentially hide.

Foreign-Aligned Oligarch Financial Channels

UNIKORNAIO further maintains that the greatest concern is not ordinary cryptocurrency ownership, legitimate foreign investment, or lawful political advocacy.

The concern is whether foreign-aligned oligarchic capital, politically exposed persons, intelligence-linked actors, offshore beneficiaries, state-connected commercial interests, or other sophisticated actors are capable of moving money into American political influence structures without adequate attribution.

The existing Section HT already identifies offshore and oligarchic financial networks as central vulnerabilities. It cites offshore secrecy structures, hidden beneficial ownership, political influence networks, and financial intermediaries as mechanisms capable of concealing foreign influence.

The same section also identifies reporting concerning oligarch-linked funds moving through shell companies, intermediaries, straw donors, lobbying firms, and political organizations.

Digital assets can potentially make these structures even more difficult to untangle because the financial path may no longer run directly:

foreign principal → bank → political recipient.

Instead, investigators may confront:

foreign or offshore capital → shell entity → digital asset → exchange → wallet → stablecoin → intermediary → investment entity → political organization or associated beneficiary.

Each additional layer increases the difficulty of determining who ultimately controlled the money and what purpose the money served.

Political Trafficking Through Financial Dependency

UNIKORNAIO's broader Section HT uses the term “trafficking of politicians” to describe an alleged system in which political officials become financially dependent upon powerful external interests and are subsequently pressured, managed, rewarded, or punished according to their compliance.

The document alleges that political influence can be exercised through campaign financing, access to donor networks, lobbying organizations, intimidation, threats of career destruction, and other forms of leverage.

It further describes what UNIKORNAIO characterizes as handler networks, alleging that lobbying organizations can function as gatekeepers that cultivate lawmakers, direct financial resources, shape policy commitments, and punish political noncompliance.

Digital assets add another potential dimension to that system.

A politician does not necessarily need to receive cryptocurrency directly for digital-asset wealth to influence political behavior.

Digital-asset-derived wealth can be converted into conventional currency and subsequently flow through:

campaign organizations;

political action committees;

Super PACs;

consulting arrangements;

corporate investments;

lobbying organizations;

media organizations;

nonprofits;

venture funds;

or other conventional financial structures.

By the time the money becomes visible within the political system, its original economic source may be difficult to reconstruct without comprehensive financial records.

UNIKORNAIO therefore maintains that source-of-funds transparency matters just as much as disclosure of the final political contribution.

The Lobbying Vulnerability

This is where the CLARITY Act becomes especially consequential.

Lobbying itself is lawful.

Political advocacy itself is lawful.

Campaign contributions made in compliance with applicable law are lawful.

But lobbying ceases to be merely a political-policy issue if competent evidence establishes that it was knowingly financed through illicit proceeds, concealed foreign money, bribery, laundering, sanctions violations, fraudulent transactions, or another unlawful financial source.

UNIKORNAIO therefore maintains that meaningful digital-asset regulation could create substantial exposure for lobbying organizations and associated intermediaries if historical records demonstrate that they knowingly participated in—or materially benefited from—illegal financial structures.

The critical question would no longer be:

“Did this lobby advocate for a particular policy?”

It would become:

“Who funded the advocacy, where did the underlying money originate, who exercised beneficial control, what did the recipients know, and did the financial arrangement violate existing law?”

That is a dramatically different inquiry.

Why Lobbyists Could Face Serious Exposure

UNIKORNAIO maintains that lobbying organizations could face particularly serious legal and reputational consequences if a comprehensive financial investigation established that lobbying activity was connected to unlawful foreign financing or a broader scheme detrimental to the United States.

That exposure could become especially significant if evidence demonstrated that lobbyists knowingly:

concealed the true source of foreign-linked funds;

participated in laundering or routing illicit proceeds;

acted as undisclosed agents of foreign principals;

coordinated political expenditures with prohibited foreign sources;

made materially false representations concerning funding or beneficial ownership;

obstructed regulatory investigations;

or participated in a continuing unlawful enterprise.

The existing Section HT already recognizes deficiencies in FARA enforcement and identifies statutory ambiguity and limited enforcement as vulnerabilities capable of permitting foreign influence to remain inadequately disclosed.

It also identifies foreign political financing cases involving straw donors and intermediaries as examples of how the true source of political money can be concealed.

The important point is that lawful lobbying does not immunize independently unlawful financing.

If money laundering, bribery, illegal foreign contributions, fraud, obstruction, or another qualifying offense is established, the existence of a lobbying organization between the original source of money and the ultimate political activity does not automatically sanitize the transaction.

Detriment to the United States Economy

The consequences become substantially more serious if investigators can demonstrate that the underlying influence campaign was not merely politically controversial but knowingly detrimental to the economic interests or national security of the United States.

Economic harm alone does not automatically create criminal liability.

But economic harm can become highly relevant evidence of motive, intent, damages, causation, and enterprise purpose where it is connected to independently unlawful conduct.

For example, if evidence established that foreign-aligned financial actors knowingly funded lobbying intended to preserve regulatory loopholes because those loopholes enabled capital flight, sanctions evasion, money laundering, market manipulation, tax avoidance, or extraction of American wealth, the economic consequences could become central to the investigation.

UNIKORNAIO maintains that investigators should therefore evaluate not only who influenced legislation, but also who economically benefited from the legislation remaining weak or ambiguous.

That inquiry could include examining whether regulatory delay enabled:

continued capital flight;

unreported foreign ownership;

concealed offshore wealth;

market manipulation;

undisclosed leverage;

inadequately collateralized digital assets;

exchange insolvency risks;

tax-base erosion;

sanctions evasion;

or continued transfer of American capital into opaque foreign-controlled structures.

If those consequences can be demonstrated through financial evidence, the lobbying surrounding the relevant regulatory decisions becomes significantly more important.

The CLARITY Act as a Regulatory “Kill Switch”

UNIKORNAIO therefore characterizes a properly constructed CLARITY Act framework as a potential regulatory “kill switch” for this type of financial opacity.

The “kill switch” is not prohibition of cryptocurrency.

It is attribution.

The entire alleged system becomes substantially more difficult to maintain when investigators can reliably connect:

source of funds → wallet → exchange → intermediary → beneficial owner → recipient → political activity → ultimate beneficiary.

Once that chain becomes reconstructable, the value of regulatory ambiguity collapses.

Shell structures become less effective.

Offshore intermediaries become easier to identify.

Digital-asset-derived political wealth becomes easier to trace.

Relationships among otherwise separate entities become easier to compare.

Foreign beneficial ownership becomes harder to disguise.

And long-term historical financial patterns become easier to reconstruct.

That is why UNIKORNAIO describes meaningful CLARITY regulation as a kill switch for opacity rather than a kill switch for cryptocurrency.

Historical Conduct Is the Critical Issue

The most consequential aspect of stronger digital-asset regulation may not be what happens after enactment.

It may be what investigators discover when historical conduct is placed under a substantially greater financial lens.

New legislation cannot retroactively criminalize activity that was lawful when performed.

But new transparency can reveal evidence concerning conduct that was already unlawful when it occurred.

This distinction is critical.

Section HT already alleges that weak regulation and fragmented exchange oversight preserved conditions in which opaque capital movement could continue. It specifically identifies digital-asset exchanges as liquidity gateways and argues that delayed or diluted regulatory reform can preserve fragmented supervision.

A more comprehensive regulatory structure could allow investigators to correlate years of:

wallet transactions;

exchange records;

banking transfers;

beneficial-ownership records;

corporate structures;

PAC expenditures;

campaign contributions;

lobbying disclosures;

foreign-agent registrations;

OTC transactions;

stablecoin flows;

and offshore financial activity.

Historical transactions that once appeared unrelated could reveal common financiers, common intermediaries, recurring recipients, coordinated timing, or shared beneficial ownership.

That is where the alleged enterprise structure becomes susceptible to forensic reconstruction.

Why Regulatory Ambiguity Matters

UNIKORNAIO maintains that regulatory ambiguity should not be viewed merely as an inconvenience for cryptocurrency companies.

Ambiguity itself can become financial infrastructure.

When agencies dispute jurisdiction, sophisticated actors can exploit the gap.

When disclosure requirements differ between platforms, beneficial ownership becomes harder to compare.

When exchanges operate through offshore structures, lawful subpoenas may become more difficult to enforce.

When no regulator possesses complete visibility, participants can exploit fragmentation.

And when political organizations advocate against stronger transparency while simultaneously receiving money derived from markets benefiting from that opacity, the financial relationships deserve careful scrutiny.

This does not mean that opposition to the CLARITY Act establishes criminal conduct.

The appropriate question is whether independent evidence shows that opposition or lobbying activity was connected to concealed financial interests or independently unlawful activity.

War, Foreign Policy, and Political Influence

UNIKORNAIO further maintains that the issue becomes particularly sensitive where digital assets, foreign political influence, oligarchic wealth, military policy, and war intersect.

Financial opacity can potentially affect decisions involving:

foreign military aid;

sanctions;

weapons transfers;

international investigations;

war-crimes accountability;

foreign-agent enforcement;

and congressional oversight.

The mere existence of lobbying concerning those subjects is not unlawful.

But where investigators identify concealed foreign funding, bribery, laundering, prohibited campaign financing, or undisclosed agency relationships, the stakes extend far beyond ordinary lobbying.

The issue becomes whether foreign-aligned money covertly influenced decisions involving American national security, economic policy, or participation in foreign conflicts.

That is precisely the type of inquiry for which transparent financial records become indispensable.

Enforcement Suppression

UNIKORNAIO further characterizes the interaction between financial opacity and political power as a potential form of enforcement suppression.

An enforcement system can be weakened without formally abolishing the law.

Investigations can be delayed.

Jurisdiction can remain fragmented.

Records can remain offshore.

Beneficial ownership can remain obscured.

Political pressure can discourage inquiries.

Lobbying can resist stronger transparency.

And by the time authorities reconstruct the transactions, the underlying assets may have moved through numerous jurisdictions and financial instruments.

The result is a system in which laws technically exist while practical enforcement remains substantially weaker than the underlying authority would suggest.

That gap benefits sophisticated actors disproportionately.

Potential RICO Significance

UNIKORNAIO maintains that this financial architecture could become relevant under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, 18 U.S.C. §§ 1961–1968, but only where competent evidence establishes the required elements.

Lobbying is not racketeering.

Political donations are not inherently racketeering.

Cryptocurrency ownership is not racketeering.

Foreign investment is not racketeering.

But if investigators establish a continuing enterprise involving qualifying predicate acts—such as bribery, wire fraud, money laundering, obstruction, extortion, or other qualifying offenses—the digital financial record can become important evidence demonstrating relationships, continuity, common purpose, and repeated conduct.

Section HT itself is expressly structured around alleged bribery, extortion, money laundering, obstruction, and RICO theories.

UNIKORNAIO therefore maintains that the strongest investigation would not begin with the assumption that every lobbying organization or political recipient committed wrongdoing.

It would begin with the money.

Follow the source.

Identify the beneficial owner.

Identify every intermediary.

Determine who knew what.

Determine what political action followed.

Determine who benefited economically.

And then determine whether the evidence establishes lawful advocacy—or a continuing unlawful enterprise.

Why the CLARITY Act Could Break the System

UNIKORNAIO therefore maintains that the CLARITY Act could be devastating to any influence network that depends upon regulatory ambiguity, opaque digital-asset ownership, offshore intermediaries, and incomplete financial attribution.

The Act does not magically eliminate corruption.

But transparency can eliminate the conditions upon which corruption depends.

If regulators can identify the beneficial owner, follow the asset, compel records from responsible intermediaries, reconstruct historical transactions, compare political expenditures with financial flows, and identify common counterparties, the concealment architecture begins to fail.

That is the kill switch.

Not shutting down digital assets.

Shutting down plausible deniability.

Not eliminating political lobbying.

Making the actual source of lobbying money visible.

Not prohibiting foreign investment.

Identifying when foreign control is being concealed.

Not criminalizing political disagreement.

Separating lawful advocacy from unlawful financing.

And not retroactively creating crimes.

Exposing evidence of conduct that may already have violated existing law.

UNIKORNAIO Conclusion

UNIKORNAIO maintains that digital assets have become a critical component of any modern investigation into political corruption, foreign influence, oligarchic finance, money laundering, enforcement suppression, and the trafficking of political power.

Section HT already identifies a system in which political influence allegedly depends upon bribery, extortion, laundering, offshore financing, handler networks, and obstruction.

Digital assets potentially provide that system with an additional layer of speed, cross-border mobility, pseudonymity, and regulatory fragmentation.

A properly designed CLARITY framework can attack the vulnerability at its weakest point:

the financial trail.

And if that trail ultimately establishes that lobbyists, intermediaries, financiers, foreign principals, oligarchic interests, or political organizations knowingly participated in illegal financing that materially harmed the United States economy or national security, then the consequences could extend far beyond ordinary regulatory penalties.

Such evidence could implicate campaign-finance law, FARA, anti-money-laundering statutes, bribery laws, fraud statutes, obstruction statutes, forfeiture provisions, and—where a qualifying enterprise and pattern of predicate activity are proven—potential Civil or Criminal RICO exposure.

That is why UNIKORNAIO considers CLARITY more than cryptocurrency legislation.

It is potentially an anti-corruption mechanism, a foreign-influence transparency mechanism, an economic-security mechanism, and a financial kill switch against networks that depend upon nobody being able to determine where the money actually came from.
