articleTitle: Graph Engineering: Stop Chaining Your Agents

text:
I head the Market Access department at Truth Social, even though that is just another way of saying that I'm selling the head start.

I provide the President with free access to 340 million Americans. I sell the ten seconds before the post to ten companies at a rate of $100,000 a month each, and the only thing I have ever needed to sell is the gap between those two figures. For most of the thirty years before I came to be here, I sold this service on Wall Street under forty different names. The name that I now use is the Truth API, and it is the most honest title that the business has ever had, and I'll explain why in a moment.

People are always referring to this as corruption. I'm going to show you, step by step, why it isn't, since I happen to enjoy doing so and because my lawyers required me to memorise the terminology.

Begin with the part that is solid. The President is not engaging in any form of sale. He publishes free of charge, for all people, at every hour, out of a love that I can only describe in those terms. The man cannot stop telling you precisely what he is about to do to the world. I do not sell his words; his words are free. I sell the gap between his words and your eyes, and that gap has never been free in this country, not a single time, not for anything deserving of being crossed.

However, it is a mistake to think that this started with him; someone has always been the one to sell the head start.

Thirty years ago I disposed of a server. Not the server itself, but the position: my client's order reached the matching engine a few millionths of a second before the rest of the market became aware that an order was in existence because the cage was 40 feet closer to the exchange's matching engine than yours. The exchange paid me for the distance. I charged a premium for it. No one regarded that as corruption. They called it colocation and included it in a brochure.

Twenty years ago I sold two seconds; a research organisation gave the nation's consumer-confidence figure to its paying elite two seconds before giving it to the general public, and in that two seconds a quick desk could turn a coin toss into a definite decision. I also sold those two seconds.

I have sold the lockup room, in which reporters hold the job report behind glass until the clock hits and a pipe that works quickly turns the embargo into a starting gun. I have sold the analyst's note before it appeared in print. I have sold my proximity to those who draw up the laws and then buy the companies which are the subject of those laws, and when they were caught they passed a law bearing their own name on it and continued to trade, and I kept on selling.

People always manage to secure the head start. I am the most skilled at doing so that has ever existed, and the Truth API is my finest achievement since, for the first time, the source is no longer leaking, whispering, or arriving two seconds early; he is now shouting for free to everybody, and yet I am still able to charge one hundred thousand dollars a month for the ten seconds that come before the shout. If you want to call it a loophole, then call it one; I refer to it as artistry and I have the profit margins to win the argument.

The point on which the critics are wrong is also the one for which I am most proud. They believe that a head start requires a crime, whereas it in fact requires the opposite. I have no use for a liar since he is unpredictable and I don't sell surprises. All I sell is certainty accompanied by a timestamp. His conviction constitutes my inventory. All I need to do is stand next to the loudest man living at the moment he exhales, and by so doing I have made the square foot next to him the most expensive in the world.

See how much the exhalation is worth. He announces that Iran has agreed to delay. The price of oil falls by $4 a barrel before the wire desk has finished phoning the Pentagon. My subscribers are already in long positions. You pick this up from a push notification. They found out from the lungs.

He announces that the tariffs are on hold. The market increases by nearly $1 trillion within the course of an afternoon. Now he has the role of the weather, so I sell the one umbrella that opens before the rain falls.

Corruption is a favour carried out in the dark. I carry out my favours through a subscription portal, using a dashboard, a rate card, and a customer-success manager called Brandon who sends you a fruit basket as soon as your funds clear the first $1 billion from the feed. They took legal action against me, of course. A press foundation and a magazine, being very serious about it, described the situation as corrupt and unconstitutional in the headline. That headline resulted in the best sales week of my career. Nothing sells a table like a velvet rope and a judge standing beside it.

This is exactly the point that I have been working towards in my entire speech, so I want you to imagine yourself in it. A head start is of no use if nobody is staying put. You can't have a fast side without a slow side to compare with. And you have already decided, in a comfortable manner, that the slow side is a pension fund in a state you have never been to.

It is you.

Throughout your life you've always been the slower part in a fast-paced trade. The layoff—that your vice president became aware of in March and you found out about in June. The increase in rent that took place the month the building changed hands, even though no one had informed the tenants weeks earlier. The plant closing the week after the executives had quietly sold it. The diagnosis code that your insurance company had already priced before your doctor had said the word out loud. You regarded all of this as bad luck. It was a product and it had a department; I manage that department.

A shop teacher who has now retired, aged 71, has one entry on page 30 of the pension fund and each Sunday morning checks his balance while having a cup of coffee, since on that day the market does not move and he is able to look at it without feeling any anxiety. In the best month of my career, the month when oil prices reached $90 as a result of the blockade, he awoke on a Sunday poorer than he had been on Saturday by an amount greater than the sum he had earned in his final full year as a teacher, and he never managed to work out which sentence had caused it. He did not receive an alert because alerts are a paid feature; he obtained the figure in the same way that the slower side always does, in a complete and finished form and far too late to be anything but a matter of arithmetic, at the speed of a citizen, that is to say, the speed of last.

Once a child who was sitting on my desk asked me whether it kept me awake. I explained to him that everybody receives the same messages. He replied to his screen without looking up, "They receive them only after it's all over; the delay is the result. You just don't include it on the invoice." After that he entered his figure for the quarter and stopped asking, just as all the others do, just as I stopped asking, just as you will stop reading this in a minute and go to check your own balance.

My own money is in a blind trust. I never trade on any of it, and here is the beautiful part: I do not have to. I sell shovels to a gold rush, and the shovel never has to find a single flake of gold. It only has to reach the dirt first. I have gotten quietly, enormously rich standing perfectly still, in daylight, with my name on the door.

All Americans have the freedom to hear the President's words, and the ten seconds prior to them cost $100,000 a month and are increasing, since there is no upper limit to the amount a person will pay in order to cease being a citizen.

All people pick up the news, with someone always being the first to do so; someone is always the one to capitalise on that early advantage, and the only difference in thirty years is that at last I've discovered a source loud enough to be able to sell the silence that comes before him and charge for it as a subscription.

There is a level higher than the one that I deal in. Although I have not been authorized to find out how much it costs, I know that it exists, that someone whom you'll never meet is already paying that price, and that on the day it becomes publicly known you'll see about it right here for free, many months after it has stopped being relevant.

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

A. “Collapse of sincerity” vs “Working constitutional speech-market” — juxtaposed refutation

Claim (Mehta): algorithms monetise performance; sincerity is dead.

Counter (law-anchored): India’s system builds, protects, and disciplines truthful communication.

Free speech spine intact: Art.19(1)(a); limits only under Art.19(2)—sovereignty, integrity (via 16th Amend., 1963), public order, decency, contempt, defamation, incitement.

Shreya Singhal (2015): struck 66A IT Act; mandated narrow tests (“incitement”, “tendency to create”). Sincerity space preserved.

Right to know fuels deliberation: PUCL v. Union (2003) & ADR (2002)—candidate disclosures as Art.19(1)(a); RTI Act 2005 operationalises truth access, not performance.

State coercion checked: Anuradha Bhasin (2020)—internet restrictions must be proportional, reasoned, reviewable. Kaushal Kishor (2023)—remedies exist for ministerial speech harm; no blanket gag on political speech.

Harmful speech contained, not chilled: Subramanian Swamy (2016) upheld criminal defamation to protect Art.21 reputation; Amish Devgan (2020) clarified hate-speech thresholds—ethics by law, not by vibe.

Platform due-diligence (not censorship): IT (Intermediary Guidelines & Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021—grievance officers, 36-hr takedown on court/LEA orders, traceability for heinous crimes; 69A IT Act blocking only via speaking orders + review (per Shreya Singhal).

Election truth-checks: Model Code of Conduct, cVIGIL, paid-news rules; ECI + SVEEP strengthen voter information.

Civic transparency expanding: Open Government Data, Proactive RTI (s.4), Social Audit (MNREGA/SSA rules)—institutionalise fact visibility.

Bottom line: The architecture prizes sincerity by rights (19(1)(a)), guardrails (19(2)), remedies (courts/RTI/ECI). The market is noisy; the constitution makes it corrigible.

A report by The Indian Express has highlighted the sharp rise in government-issued blocking orders to social media platforms between March and July, during the period of the CJP student protests.

Most of these directions were issued through the Sahyog portal, a government platform used by Central and state agencies to send blocking notices to social media companies. The report says many of these orders were issued under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, 2000, which requires intermediaries to remove unlawful content to retain their legal protection. These are separate from blocking directions issued under Section 69A of the IT Act.

The report also says Meta has integrated its API with Sahyog to comply with the government’s 2–3-hour deadline, potentially allowing content flagged through government directions to be blocked automatically without a separate human review.

Digital-rights advocates have raised concerns about this mechanism and its implications for due process and freedom of expression.

The Silent Emergency: Eleven Years Under the Shadow of Control

India, the land of a billion vibrant voices, is grappling with a chilling silence. For eleven years under the PM, we've witnessed an

"Undeclared Emergency@11"

—no declared curfews, no tanks, but a steady erosion of our democratic freedoms. This is the story of a Nation fighting for its soul, where the cost of speaking out grows heavier daily.

The Press in Chains
Our Fourth Estate, once a beacon of truth, now falters under relentless pressure. V-Dem and Freedom House 2025 reports label India an “electoral autocracy,” ranked “partly free.” The Press Freedom Index places us at 159/176, near Somalia’s shadow. Honest journalists face arrests, raids, and intimidation for daring to question. Laws like UAPA and sedition are weaponized, branding critics “terrorists” without trial. Media houses face raids, their voices stifled. Modi’s 11-year tenure without a single press conference speaks volumes—hate speech thrives, but truth is jailed.

Homes Turned to Rubble
Bulldozers roar across India, not for progress but as tools of vengeance. Homes, often of minorities or dissenters, are demolished in displays of state power. Families stand amid rubble, targeted for their identity or beliefs. Ministers spewing hate are rewarded, while citizens live in fear. This isn’t the India we fought for.

The Digital Gag
In the age of X, FB, Insta, and YouTube, where voices once soared, dissent is now caged. Content creators and tweeters face arrests for “misinformation” or “inciting unrest.” Over 20,000 independent voices have been silenced, their crime often a post challenging the regime. This is a democracy where keyboards are as dangerous as megaphones.

Opposition Under Siege
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has become a weapon to intimidate opposition leaders, with raids targeting those who refuse to bow to the BJP. Homes and offices of opposition figures are stormed, cases piled up to coerce them into joining the ruling party or face relentless harassment. This blatant misuse of agencies undermines democracy, turning dissent into a dangerous act.

Puppet Election Commission
The Election Commission, once a pillar of democratic integrity, now dances to the tune of the BJP. The removal of the Chief Justice of India from the selection committee for appointing Election Commissioners has raised alarms about its independence. This move, critics argue, ensures a pliable EC, ready to tilt the electoral scales. Free and fair elections, the heartbeat of democracy, now pulse under the shadow of control.

The Leader’s Shadow
Modi’s image dominates—billboards, screens, even vaccine certificates and rail tickets. Supporters call it leadership; we see a cult stifling dissent. Parliament weakened, constitutional bodies eroded, divisive figures glorified—this is a five-fold assault on our democracy. BJP invokes 1975’s Emergency to deflect, but today’s control needs no formal name. It’s a slow, silent strangulation of our freedoms.

Nation’s Resolve
Fifty years ago, India resisted the 1975 Emergency. Today, the shackles are subtler but real. Jailed journalists, bulldozed homes, silenced voices, ED raids on opposition leaders, and a compromised Election Commission tell of a democracy under siege. As Modi marks “Samvidhan Hatya Diwas,” we say the real threat to our Constitution is now—unnamed, insidious, but ever-present.

India stands at a crossroads. Will we reclaim our chorus of voices or let silence prevail? The fight for our democracy lies in the courage of those who speak, write, and dream of a free tomorrow. 

#UndeclaredEmergency #SaveDemocracy

WHEN THE ELECTION WATCHDOG IS ASKED TO WATCH ITSELF

The Election Commission is supposed to be the referee of India’s elections. But what happens when citizens begin asking whether the referee is applying the rules equally?

Transparency activist Anjali Bhardwaj, in The Probe, raises precisely this uncomfortable question: are complaints of Model Code of Conduct violations being handled with the same urgency when they concern opposition leaders and leaders of the ruling party?

These are serious allegations—not facts that should be accepted merely because they are made in a video. But they deserve answers.

The 2019 election provides a telling historical example. NaMo TV, a channel devoted to Narendra Modi’s speeches and pro-BJP content, appeared during the election period. The Election Commission eventually ordered that political content without the required certification be removed, after opposition parties complained.

The larger democratic question is therefore not simply whether the ECI sometimes acts.

It is whether it acts consistently, promptly and without fear or favour.

Because democracy does not merely depend on voting.

It depends on whether every contestant believes that the rules will be enforced equally.

When an opposition leader faces immediate scrutiny while allegations involving those in power appear to move slowly—or disappear into institutional silence—the damage is larger than any individual complaint.

It begins to erode something much more precious:

public trust in the referee.

And once citizens stop believing that the electoral referee is neutral, the ballot box itself begins to carry the weight of suspicion.

The Election Commission therefore owes the country more than decisions.

It owes us transparency about the decisions—and equal accountability for everyone who seeks power.

text:
🔆Telecommunications Bill 2023

✅Recently, the government introduced the Telecommunications Bill 2023 in the Lok Sabha. It seeks to repeal the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, the Indian Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933, and the Telegraph Wires (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1950. It also amends the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) Act, 1997.

📍What are the Key Provisions of Telecommunications Bill 2023?

✅Authorisation for Telecom-related Activities: Prior authorisation from the central government will be required to provide telecommunication services, establish, operate, maintain, or expand telecommunications networks, or possess radio equipment.
Existing licenses will continue to be valid for the period of their grant, or for five years, where the period is not specified.
✅Assignment of Spectrum: Spectrum will be assigned by auction, except for specified uses, where it will be allocated on an administrative basis. These include purposes such as national security and defense, disaster management, weather forecasting, transport, satellite services such as DTH and satellite telephony, and BSNL, MTNL, and public broadcasting services.
✅Satellite Internet Allotments: The Bill introduces provisions for allocating spectrum to satellite Internet providers like OneWeb (supported by Bharti) and U.S.-based companies such as SpaceX's Starlink.
✅Powers of Interception and Search: Messages or a class of messages between two or more persons may be intercepted, monitored, or blocked on certain grounds.
✅Powers to Specify Standards: The central government may prescribe standards and assessments for telecom equipment, infrastructure, networks, and services.
✅Right of Way: Facility providers may seek a right of way over public or private property to establish telecom infrastructure.
✅Appointments to TRAI: The Bill amends the TRAI Act to also allow individuals with: at least 30 years of professional experience to serve as the chairperson, and at least 25 years of professional experience to serve as members.
✅Digital Bharat Nidhi: The Universal Service Obligation Fund has been established under the 1885 Act to provide for telecom services in underserved areas.
✅Regulation of OTT Apps: It has removed over-the-top (OTT) services and apps from the definition of telecommunication services, in a big relief to communication service providers such as WhatsApp and Telegram.
✅Adjudication Process: The central government will appoint an adjudicating officer to conduct inquiries and pass orders against civil offenses under the Bill.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

On the night of 14th August 1947, a flag flew on Jawaharlal Nehru's car as it went over Raisina Hill. It was the first time the tricolour we know today was ever flown.

That flag had been stitched under the supervision of a 28 year old woman.

Her name was Surayya Tyabji.

She was born in 1919 in Hyderabad. She was a painter. Her work was later shown in London and in Jakarta. She was married to Badruddin Tyabji, a civil servant who was part of the group working on what independent India would look like.

Everyone had assumed the flag was settled. Pingali Venkayya had designed the tricolour used by the Congress, with Gandhi's charkha in the middle. It had been carried through the freedom movement for over 20 years.

Then, weeks before independence, a problem was raised. That flag was a party flag. A country that was about to include everyone could not fly the symbol of one political party.

So the design had to be redone, quickly.

The Tyabjis were given the job.

They replaced the charkha with the Ashoka Chakra, the wheel from the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath. The reason was simple and deliberate. Ashoka belonged to all Indians, and to no party.

Their daughter Laila Tyabji has written the family's account of it. Her mother drew the graphic version. The printing press at the Viceregal Lodge made the impressions. Everyone approved.

The English historian Trevor Royle recorded in his book that the flag which flew on Nehru's car that night had been made by Tyabji's wife.

On 22nd July 1947 the design was accepted by the Constituent Assembly.

A report in the Times of India in January 1950 described that first flag as having been presented to the nation by the women of India at the midnight session of the Constituent Assembly on 14th August 1947.

Before the flag, the same couple had worked on the national emblem. Nehru asked Badruddin to do something about it because he had an eye for these things. Surayya drew the version of the 4 lions that has been on every Indian government document since.

She was 28 years old.

She died in 1978 in Mumbai.

Her daughter has said that neither of her parents ever felt they had designed the national emblem. They felt they had only reminded India of something that had always been part of its identity.

Official records of the Constituent Assembly do not name individual contributors, so most textbooks still credit only Venkayya, and his work genuinely came first.

But today, when the flag goes up, look at the wheel in the middle of it.

A young Muslim woman put it there, on purpose, so that no Indian would be left out of it.

IFF’s Statement on the Blocking of X Account of the Cockroach Janta Party

22 May 2026

On May 21, 2026, the X (formerly Twitter) handle of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) (@CJP_2029) was withheld in India under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. IFF strongly condemns the blocking of the CJP’s X handle as a blatant misuse of State power and an arbitrary and disproportionate attempt to stifle freedom of speech and expression, a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India.

According to reporting by The Indian Express on May 22, 2026, the blocking directions were issued on the basis of inputs from the Intelligence Bureau citing threat to the sovereignty of India, jeopardizing national security and the fact that the account was gaining traction among young people. Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000, empowers the Central government to direct any Government agency or intermediary to block public access to information in the “interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, defence of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States or public order or for preventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offence”. While Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 permits blocking on limited grounds, these grounds cannot be vague and speculative. Political commentary and criticism of public institutions are protected forms of speech under the Indian Constitution. The popularity of the account or the fact that the account mobilised young people through political expression cannot by itself be treated as a threat to national security.

The Indian Express’s report mentions that “blocking orders are issued under a confidential framework” which is deeply concerning. We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court of India upheld Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) on the basis that it is a narrowly drawn provision with several safeguards in place, including written reasoning for the blocking that is subject to legal challenge. State censorship like the blocking of CJP’s X account propagates opacity and provides affected users with no options for redressal, thereby effectively defeating these safeguards. IFF calls on the Union government to ensure timely notices are provided to affected users along with clear grounds and avenues for remedy.

IFF has previously explained how users whose constitutional rights are being infringed upon by the State can seek restoration of their blocked content. If you are an Indian social media user or journalist whose content has been blocked due to a government order, please write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in.

Yesterday, The West Australian ran a piece predicting voter "election fatigue" for West Australian’s in early 2025, as West Aussies head to the polls for both State and Federal elections.

The article speculated on rising political stars but, true to form, The West Australian stuck to the two major parties, sidelining alternatives as usual.

The 2021 WA State election handed the McGowan/Cook Labor government unmatched political power and wealth, which they repeatedly wielded in the Legislative Council (Upper House) to push through draconian legislation—often at the expense of the WA public.

To make matters worse, amid the pandemic hype, former Premier Mark McGowan quietly revamped the rules for how parties and independents can contest Upper House elections—ensuring WA Labor retains a firm grip on passing laws to cement its power.

The electoral reform was a major pre-election betrayal, with Mark McGowan breaking his promise to the WA public. 

Despite assuring voters McGowan had no plans for changes, he went ahead anyway, proving his word false.

As we head into the next election, it’s crucial for voters to know how to make their vote count. 

Without informed choices, we face more of the same—soaring infrastructure costs, rising living expenses, housing and healthcare shortages, and a complete departure from the "gold standard transparency" WA Labor promised.

Now, before the “Vote the Majors last” comments roll in, let’s be clear: it’s not that simple.

To make your vote effective especially for the Upper House, you need to understand the nuances. 

Voting above the line should ideally be numbered 1 to 6, avoiding the majors entirely, if at all possible.

But here’s the catch: you also need to know how minor party preferences flow.

For instance, the Animal Justice Party is likely to preference The Greens  which will ultimately benefit Labor. 

Make your vote count with informed choices and given the time left to the state election, voters would be best placed examining the political parties that “made” the overly onerous requirements to register a political party.

In Western Australia, the Libertarian Party WA is emerging as a credible choice for West Australian voters disillusioned with the status quo, the two major parties.

Pauline Hanson’s One Nation (WA) seemed poised for success, but recent months—and especially the past week—have exposed significant cracks.

PHON WA leader Rod Caddies, absent since the last state election preoccupied with his now-failed “People’s First Party,” only resurfacing after the previous PHON WA team successfully registered the party with the WA Electoral Commission in February this year.

Caddie’s pandemic-era silence raises serious questions about his leadership and commitment, with his recent track record making one thing clear—transparency and accountability aren’t his priorities.

A recent exposé by indie media @Whats_Newsss on "X" has added fuel to the fire. The piece focused on Parminder Singh, #3 candidate for PHON WA on Caddie’s Upper House ticket, who faced heavy criticism in a telephone interview that has amassed over 80,000 views in just days, sparking widespread backlash.

Watch here: https://t.co/TJi3QOuhuh

Numerous commenters on “X” highlighted Singh’s controversial stances on immigration, which directly conflict with PHON’s Zero Net Immigration policy.

Singh advocated for increased immigration from India, claiming such migrants “bring the money” and championing multiculturalism. 

He also dismissed concerns about economic recession and criticized Australians for “not wanting to work.”

Caddies denied any record of Singh’s posts on socials and comments supporting higher immigration and doubled down in a video response alongside his "captain's pick," Parminder Singh. 

In the video, Caddies insisted Singh is aligned with PHON’s Zero Net Immigration.

Watch here: https://t.co/gervnSEZHR

A claim that quickly unravelled, as numerous "X" users provided evidence of Singh’s Facebook posts promoting the exact opposite of PHON’s platform.

Singh’s Facebook account has since undergone a rapid purge, with incriminating content erased.

Notably, Parminder Singh’s Facebook changed from- Parminder Singh – Candidate for State Legislative Council to Parminder Singh Manji, with only the profile picture left unchanged.

A move Rod Caddies denies ever took place.

However, this claim drew further scrutiny.

When FMWA pressed Caddies with a straightforward question: “As PHON WA leader, do you still support Parminder Singh’s candidacy?”

Caddies responded not with accountability but with personal attacks against the independent journalist who raised the questions and blocked on social media.

Singh's candidacy has put a spotlight on One Nation’s candidate vetting and commitment to core policies, raising serious questions about the process and leadership transparency.

Before this "captain's pick," more questions than answers have emerged:

• What did the “selectors” know about Singh’s clear stance advocating for increased immigration?

• If nothing was known, doesn’t this expose serious flaws in the pre-selection process?

• If selectors were aware of Singh’s stance conflicting with PHON’s zero net immigration policy, what’s really going on behind the scenes?

The PHON WA base and the voting public deserve clear answers—and fast.

With these controversies unfolding, the Western Australia state election promises to be one to watch closely.

The government has all data on Aadhaar, Voter IDs, Passport so why is this information relevant for a census?

quotedTweet.text:
IFF has written to the Union Home Secretary and the Census Commissioner over the household survey notified four days ago. Serial numbers 36 to 40 ask for mobile, Aadhaar, voter ID and passport numbers, not whether you have them, unlike serial number 40, which only asks about availability of a driving license.

IFF supports enumerating caste for substantive equality. But pairing Aadhaar numbers with religion and caste sits against the Aadhaar Act's bar on profiling, and the questionnaire itself remains unpublished.
We are not opposed to the census. We want it conducted in a way that earns public trust.

Other countries have adopted stronger safeguards. UN census principles emphasise that individual information should not be linked to other government databases for non-statistical purposes. Countries including Canada and Australia avoid collecting certain identifiers or keep contact information separate from statistical data. Germany’s Constitutional Court has also rejected census-to-register linkage. (7/8)

IFF supports the inclusion of caste in Census 2027. Reliable caste data can be essential to understanding inequality and advancing constitutional commitments to equality. But counting caste does not require creating identity-linked records. We have asked the government to delete unnecessary identifiers, guarantee that data will not be linked with other databases, publish security and retention safeguards, and make any retained fields expressly voluntary. (8/8)

Instagram alone accounted for over half of these orders, much of it during the period of the Delhi students' protests against exam leaks.

We had filed an RTI seeking exactly this kind of information: the total number of blocking/removal directions issued through the Sahyog portal, a month wise and platform wise break up, the legal provisions invoked, and the authorities issuing them.
